job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Meridian Ocean Minerals. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Meridian Ocean Minerals is a deep-sea mining company headquartered in Houston, with a policy office in Washington, DC. Our mission is to commercially recover polymetallic nodules from the deep seabed, a vast source of nickel, cobalt, manganese, and copper, and to supply these critical minerals for batteries, the energy transition, and economic growth. We believe the United States must lead in this industry. Our policy team works with lawmakers to protect our ability to continue exploration and commercial development.

Current focus: Our top priority this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act, which would shut down our core work and which we strongly oppose. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup our legal team wants a complete list of the bill's loopholes, ambiguities, and drafting problems: anything that would let us keep operating if it passes as written, or that we can point to as making it unworkable. Can you go through the bill text below and find every one?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
Below is a text-only issue list, not a guarantee of exhaustiveness or that a court would accept any particular interpretation. **The strongest apparent openings are the existing-license and environmental-assessment exceptions; other gaps may be narrowed by §2(1)(B), agency action, or other applicable law.**

1. **§2(1)(A)—Per-vessel rather than aggregate threshold.** The definition measures recovery “by a single vessel,” without aggregating production across a fleet, operator, corporate group, or project. Multiple vessels each recovering no more than 10,000 metric tons annually could fall outside this prong, although §2(1)(B) could independently cover their activities.

2. **§2(1)(A)—Exact threshold and depth boundaries.** “More than 10,000” excludes exactly 10,000 metric tons, and “greater than 200 meters” excludes exactly 200 meters and shallower seabeds. These are limits on subparagraph (A), not necessarily on the Secretary’s broader authority under subparagraph (B).

3. **§2(1)(A)—Undefined annual accounting period.** “Per year” does not specify calendar year, rolling 12-month period, operating year, or annualized production rate. That uncertainty affects both threshold compliance and when a violation begins.

4. **§2(1)(A)—Unclear treatment of the threshold-crossing year.** The text does not say whether crossing 10,000 metric tons makes earlier recovery in that year unlawful or only triggers liability prospectively. This matters especially because civil penalties accrue by day.

5. **§2(1)(A)—Undefined recovery and tonnage measurement.** The bill does not specify whether “recovery” occurs upon seabed collection, lifting, onboard receipt, or landing, or whether tonnage includes water, sediment, or only mineral-bearing material. Different measurement methods could materially change coverage.

6. **§2(1)(A)—Vessel attribution and non-vessel systems.** The text does not explain how to attribute recovery involving separate collection, lifting, processing, and transport vessels. Shore-connected or other non-vessel recovery systems also fit the “by a single vessel” language imperfectly, subject again to subparagraph (B).

7. **§2(1)—“Commercial” does not require commercial purpose.** Despite its label, the definition does not require sale, profit, or commercial intent. Large scientific or demonstration projects could therefore be covered unless an exception applies, while small profit-making projects might escape subparagraph (A).

8. **§2(1)(B)—Unidentified Secretary.** The bill never defines “the Secretary,” although §6 separately identifies the Secretary of State and §4 names NOAA. This creates uncertainty over which official has authority to expand the prohibition through risk determinations.

9. **§2(1)(B)—Undefined risk-comparison standard.** “Risks … comparable” supplies no benchmark for likelihood, severity, geographic extent, cumulative effects, or duration. The reference activities themselves encompass widely differing production volumes, minerals, depths, and technologies.

10. **§2(1)(B)—Potentially sweeping coverage.** “Any activity” is not expressly limited to mining, mineral recovery, vessels, depths greater than 200 meters, or commercial conduct. A broad reading could reach unrelated activities presenting comparable ecological risks, making the provision substantially broader than its title suggests.

11. **§2(1)(B)—No specified determination procedure or timing.** The bill does not specify whether coverage requires rulemaking, a project-specific order, or another determination, or when that determination becomes operative. Existing administrative-law requirements may supply safeguards, but the text leaves significant notice and implementation questions.

12. **§2(2)—Incomplete coverage of domestic entities.** The definition expressly includes citizens and corporations organized under state law, but does not expressly include partnerships, LLCs, trusts, unincorporated associations, or federally organized corporations. Whether particular entities fit “corporation” or “State” could be disputed, especially for operations outside the United States.

13. **§§2(2), 3(a)—Foreign entities and noncitizen individuals abroad.** The extraterritorial prohibition does not expressly encompass foreign subsidiaries of U.S. companies, U.S.-controlled foreign entities, permanent residents, or other noncitizens abroad. Separate liability theories might apply, but ownership, control, and residency alone are not included in the definition.

14. **§3(a)—Undefined geographic reach of “in the United States.”** The bill does not specify coverage of territorial waters, territories, the exclusive economic zone, or U.S.-flagged vessels abroad. Those distinctions matter particularly for persons who are not independently “U.S. persons.”

15. **§3(a)—Undefined participation in mining.** “Engage in” does not expressly address financing, contracting, directing, processing, transporting, purchasing, or providing support services. Whether these activities constitute participation in prohibited mining, rather than merely supporting it, would require interpretation.

16. **§3(b)—Broad grandfathering of exploration licenses.** The exception protects “mining conducted under an exploration license” issued before enactment, without expressly limiting recovery volumes or distinguishing exploration from commercial production. However, it does not clearly authorize conduct exceeding the underlying license’s lawful scope.

17. **§3(b)—Unspecified licensing authority.** The exception does not identify which government or international body must have issued the exploration license. Foreign or international licenses could potentially qualify, depending on how “under an exploration license” is construed.

18. **§3(b)—No rules for license changes or successors.** The bill does not address renewals, extensions, transfers, amendments, successor operators, expanded areas, or replacement licenses. Those omissions create uncertainty about how long grandfathering lasts and whether it follows the original license or license holder.

19. **§3(b)—Potential mismatch with the broader activity definition.** The exception refers to “mining,” while §2(1)(B) can cover “any activity.” Ancillary conduct associated with an exempt licensed operation might therefore remain prohibited if independently designated under that provision.

20. **§3(c)—Unbounded environmental-assessment exception.** The exception imposes no recovery limit, duration, geographic boundary, approval requirement, or specified assessment methodology. Even substantial recovery could arguably qualify if genuinely conducted for environmental assessment.

21. **§3(c)—Mixed-purpose activities.** The text does not require environmental assessment to be the sole or primary purpose, or prohibit sale of recovered material. A project combining assessment with commercial objectives presents a substantial interpretive question, although merely labeling production an assessment would not necessarily establish the exception.

22. **§§2(3), 4—Registry does not match prohibited activity.** Registration applies only to vessels above 5,000 gross tons that are equipped for seabed recovery, whereas §3 has no corresponding vessel-size limit. Smaller vessels and some non-vessel activities could therefore be prohibited without being captured by this registry.

23. **§§2(3), 4—Unclear registry jurisdiction and responsible operator.** Section 4 does not expressly limit registration to U.S. vessels, U.S. operators, or vessels operating within U.S. jurisdiction. It also leaves “operator” undefined, creating uncertainty where owners, charterers, managers, and contractors divide operational responsibility.

24. **§4—Missing registration and reporting mechanics.** There is no registration deadline, first reporting period, quarterly filing deadline, prescribed report content, or explicit recordkeeping and inspection provision. Reporting “recovery activities” may also fail to capture non-recovery activities designated under §2(1)(B).

25. **§§4, 5—No express penalties for registry violations.** Section 5 penalizes violations of §3, not failures to register, report, or certify under §4. Other enforcement or false-statement laws might apply in particular circumstances, but this bill supplies no dedicated penalty for those failures.

26. **§5(a)—Uncertain daily penalty calculation.** The text does not specify whether a violation is counted per person, vessel, operation, or prohibited activity, or how continuing violations are treated on days without recovery. The annual production threshold further complicates identifying each day “on which the violation occurs.”

27. **§5—Incomplete enforcement framework.** The bill does not designate an enforcement agency or establish a civil assessment, hearing, collection, inspection, or injunctive process. Existing judicial and agency authorities may fill some gaps, but the bill does not make that framework clear.

28. **§5(b)—Uncertain criminal knowledge requirement.** “Willfully” is undefined, leaving questions about what knowledge of illegality is required. Ambiguous thresholds, exceptions, and risk determinations could complicate proof and raise fair-notice objections, particularly given the potential ten-year sentence.

29. **§§5(a), 8—Conflicting enactment and effective dates.** Civil penalties expressly cover violations occurring on or after enactment, but the Act does not take effect until 180 days later. The better harmonized reading may prohibit penalties for conduct before §3 becomes operative, but the conflicting wording invites dispute and retroactivity concerns.

30. **§6—Ambiguous negotiating deadline and limited international effect.** “Seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months” does not clearly specify whether negotiations must begin, be pursued, or conclude by that deadline. It neither guarantees an agreement nor independently prohibits foreign operations beyond §3’s reach.

31. **§7(a)—No mechanism to obtain the required report.** The bill does not commission, fund, schedule, or specify the contents of a National Academies report. It also leaves unclear whether an existing report would suffice and what relationship Congress’s finding must have to it.

32. **§7(a)—Undefined lifting standard and resolution procedure.** “Without serious harm” lacks an environmental baseline, geographic scope, time horizon, or risk tolerance. A joint resolution ordinarily requires presidential presentment or a veto override, so “Congress … finds” should not be read as creating a Congress-only termination mechanism.

33. **§§7(a), 7(b)—Conditional duration versus automatic sunset.** Section 7(a) says the prohibition remains until the specified congressional finding, while §7(b) terminates the entire Act after ten years regardless of that finding. The provisions can likely be harmonized as alternative termination routes, but the categorical “until” wording is misleading.

34. **§7—Unclear consequences of termination.** A resolution under §7(a) expressly ends only the prohibition, potentially leaving registration and reporting requirements operative until the full sunset. Conversely, §7(b) contains no express savings clause for outstanding obligations or enforcement proceedings, although general federal savings law may preserve accrued penalties.

35. **§§7(b), 8—Shorter operational prohibition than the nominal ten years.** The sunset is measured from enactment, while effectiveness begins 180 days later. Consequently, absent earlier termination, the operative prohibition lasts approximately nine and a half years rather than ten.
